Mr. Speaker, my purpose in entering into this debate at the present time is to set the record straight for those serious students of parliament and for historians, political scientists and political pundits.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I should like to draw attention to the fact that this supply motion is a great concession to the pleas of the government. We in the opposition are forgoing what would normally be required, namely, five supply motions before the estimates for the fiscal year 196566 could be passed by the house. Under the regular rules six supply motions are in order and supply can be entered upon and the estimates brought before the house only by that means. The government requested that we telescope the remaining five supply motions and consent to the introduction of all the remaining estimates at the conclusion of this debate.
It is interesting, sir, to note that in the session of 1962-63 this proposal was made by myself as house leader to the house leaders of the parties in the house in that parliament and it was rejected. The same suggestion was put forward to the House of Commons by the Prime Minister of that day and was rejected by the opposition. I point that out to indicate the intransigent attitude that was shown by
February 1, 1966

the Liberal party in 1962-63 and the co-operative attitude of the Conservative party at this particular time. When students of parliament are reviewing the session of 1962-63, which they will occasionally, I hope they will also have a look at this particular period in Canada's history.
There is a great similarity between the two periods, and I should like to indicate the contrast between the attitude of our party now in opposition and the attitude of the Liberal party in 1962-63 when it was in opposition. We were faced then with prolonged and deliberate obstruction of the business of the house and parliament was virtually brought to a standstill. Let us not overlook the fact that the subject of supply is of vital importance to parliament. The control of expenditure is something which has to be viewed with responsibility and there is a danger that parliament is losing its control over expenditures on the part of the government.
This loss of control stems from the attitude of the Liberal party over the last several years. It is a very serious matter and parliament must be cautious in the future to see that the blank cheque which has been given to this government for 10 months now does not become an established practice.
There seems to be an erroneous impression that parliament exists only for the passage of legislation. I suggest that its function with regard to taxation and expenditure is more important although, of course, legislation is vital because of the requirements of changing conditions. Then there is the grand inquest of the nation which is carried on here as we investigate the actions of the executive. But what taxes are to be applied and how that tax money is to be spent are matters that really concern parliament and in the interests of our constituents we must be careful to see that there is no waste of taxpayers' money and no careless expenditure.
Under the situation that has prevailed for the last two or three years control of parliament over the executive has been slackened. We are now in the situation that for the fiscal year 1965-66 not one single estimate of the main estimates has been passed by parliament. This is due to the lack of organization of government business on the part of the government, as I will show when I deal with the session last year from April to June 30, coupled with the failure of the government to summon parliament early after the election
Supply-Mr. Churchill
of November 8, with the consequence that they have now boxed themselves into this position.
I repeat, not a single estimate of the main estimates has been passed by the House of Commons. Two supplementary estimates were passed in the month of June at the request of the government and with the cooperation of the opposition because we realized that they were essential at that time.
Where is the government headed, Mr. Speaker? They have had to come crawling to us cap in hand asking us for assistance which we could have refused. It was refused to us in the session of 1962-63. We could have refused and claimed our right to have five more supply motions. We do not have to pass the estimates for 1965-66 in one day or in a few hours. This is our opportunity to find out how the departments have been administered.
We have not had an accounting to this house by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) for two years. We let him off in 1963 when his estimates were those we had prepared when we formed the government. This is rather strange, but we exhibited some sympathy for the Minister of Transport in 1963 because of a report at that time that his health was not very good and so we did not press him.
In 1964 his estimates came before the House of Commons in November, when we were working under an allocation of time schedule, and were not subject to discussion at all. Throughout the course of the year 1965 we have not had a word from him with regard to the expenditures of the Department of Transport.
That is only one example, Mr. Speaker. I could go down the list and show that we have not had an accounting to this house of the activities of ministers of the government, and this has gone on now for almost two years. It would be interesting to hear a report from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hel-lyer). In 1964 his estimates were subject to the guillotine procedure and were not discussed here on the floor of the House of Commons. We have not had a report from the Minister of National Defence in the year 1965. So you can see, sir, the importance of the discussion of supply upon which we have now entered and the importance of our taking adequate time when the estimates are before us commencing on Thursday to see just what has been going on with regard to the expenditure of the taxpayers' money.

Supply-Mr. Churchill
That is the present situation. We are not moving any amendment, again by agreement, in order that we may proceed on Wednesday with the passage of this supply motion and the calling of the remaining estimates department by department.
Now let us look at another factor, Mr. Speaker. What has the government been living on in the interval? It had interim supply granted to it, which is quite normal every year. Interim supply is normally granted for the months of April, May, June and July and until the main estimates have been passed by the house. We granted to the government at the end of June a four months' extension of interim supply carrying them to the end of October. Relying on the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on June 27, we expected to be called back in September to complete the work of that particular session.

speechtext:
Yes, September 27 was the date that he set. I think the Leader of the House was relying on that word from the Prime Minister. But in the interval the Prime Minister received advice from various sources and made a decision himself, or so he claimed. When he announced the election on the night he appeared on television he said: This is my decision and mine alone. Yet we have had all sorts of apologists subsequently telling us that the Prime Minister was given bad advice and that these people have acted the part of flagellants and taken the blame on their own shoulders. Be this as it may, the Prime Minister, having promised the country that the house would meet on September 27, saw fit to call an election. In the interim the government had supply granted for seven months of the year. Subsequently it used Governor General's warrants.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Now that parliament is reassembled this must come to an end and the government is obliged to get the consent of parliament in order to meet any further expenditures. May I point out that during election years the discussion of estimates has always been restricted because of the intervention of the election. That is normal practice. Following the election the house has proceeded somewhat speedily to deal with the estimates which could not be dealt with earlier. Three years ago almost to the day I drew the attention of the house to a survey I had

made. I think I will put this on Hansard again just for historical purposes. Here are my words:
In the year 1945 the house assembled in the spring. An election was held in June and the house reassembled in the fall. The same was done in 1949 with an election in June. In 1957 there was an election in June and in 1962 there was an election in June. If you look at the way in which the estimates were handled in those four calendar years you will find that parliament passed interim supply for a nine month period in 1945 before the main estimates were dealt with. In 1945 the opposition was a responsible opposition; it was the Conservative party. In December of that year they dealt with the estimates in co-operation with the government very quickly and passed them in a very short time.
In fact, in the last six days of December that year they passed most of the estimates, but they sat long hours late at night past midnight and early in the morning. In 1949 interim supply was granted for eight months. Again there was a responsible opposition, the Conservative party, and that responsible opposition, co-operating with the government of the day, passed the main estimates in the last few days of the session in the fall of that year. They took 15 days to pass the estimates.
That was on February 4, 1963. I went on:
I suggest to you that that situation should have prevailed in the year 1962. There was a spring session, then an election in June, and then a fall session. A responsible opposition would have co-operated with the government and passed the main estimates in the fall of 1962.
This, I suggest, is the method by which interim supply and main estimates were dealt with in the past during election years. But after the election of 1962 the Liberal party, bent on obstruction and on downgrading parliament, refused to follow the practice of former years and declined to pass any estimates in the fall of 1962. We had the normal supply motion. We called six departments and placed them in front of the house. But the Liberal opposition refused to pass a single estimate. In December of that year we asked and were compelled to ask for interim supply for the month of January because the main estimates had not been passed.
The Liberal opposition spent six full days on interim supply in December, 1962. Ninety per cent of the time interim supply is passed in half a day or a day and a half. But in that year the Liberal opposition consumed six full days before granting interim supply for January. During those six days we could have passed and dealt with the main estimates for that fiscal year. But they were bent on destroying the government of the day and on downgrading parliament.
Now let us look at the present situation. Chickens come home to roost. Here we have the Liberal party forming the government.
February 1, 1966

The Liberal party is now faced with the necessity of getting parliamentary approval of the estimates for the fiscal year 1965-66 which runs out on March 31. They have had to come to us and ask for a telescoping of the supply motions, which we have granted. Next week they have to come hat in hand, on bended knee, and ask for interim supply for the month of February. This is the case because we cannot pass these main estimates just on Thursday and Friday of this week. There is too much money involved. The main estimates for the fiscal year 1965-66 run to more than $7 billion. We want to know how the money granted so far has been spent and what is proposed with regard to the balance which is required and with regard to the final supplementary estimates which have been placed before us.
We cannot deal with this in two days. Consequently, some time next week the Leader of the House-it will be the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) actually-will have to ask parliament for interim supply for the month of February. That will be the eleventh month of the fiscal year. Let me point out the dangers which are involved. This is a serious matter. When you reach the point where you have to ask for interim supply at the end of the tenth month of the year you have reached the critical moment. Here is a statement which was made a few years ago when that point had been reached, as found on page 2739 of Hansard for December 17, 1962:
Either the government will come before us with some kind of omnibus bill asking us to vote all the estimates in one swift action because by then the government will argue it is time to start talking about the estimates for 1963-64, or because parliament stands on its feet and because parliament seeks to debate these items there will either be prorogation of the session so the government can use Governor General's warrants or there will be dissolution and an election. I do not know which of these various courses is going to be followed, but I do know that no matter which one of them is pursued we are going to witness the fiscal year 1962-63 as one in which parliament and the House of Commons in particular did not have its traditional, its constitutional right to discuss the items in the estimates as the Minister of Finance on December 12 assured us we would have. Not because there was anything lacking in the assurance he gave, but rather because of the time that has been taken with a long summer interval when there was no session of parliament and the failure of the government to organize the business of this session, we are going to be in the position where one of the main rights that is supposed to belong to parliament will have been lost.
That main right to which I am referring is parliament's control over the purse strings. That is what we are supposed to have, not the kind of government in which the executive makes all the
Supply-Mr. Churchill decisions and spends all the money but the kind of government we are supposed to have is one in which, whatever else the executive may be able to do by order in council, by executive action, control of the purse remains with parliament itself. We are going to lose that control in this fiscal year 1962-63 either by the passage of time or by dissolution and an election.
Then, listen to this:
If we go on, if we get another of these supply bills for an eleventh twelfth and another for a twelfth twelfth, it will be pointed up so that everyone in the country will be able to see that parliament's control of the purse strings has been taken away.
That was the danger in December, 1962, when we were asking for interim supply for the tenth month of the fiscal year. The heavens were to fall. Everything was going to come to an end. Parliament was being destroyed. Those words, I expect, will be repeated now by the hon. member who used them, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I assume he will stand up during the course of this debate and draw parliament's attention to the danger which he saw then and which is compounded now because we are facing interim supply next week for the eleventh month of the fiscal year. In fact, it may well be that we shall have to consider interim supply for the month of March which would be the twelfth month of the fiscal year.
He was not the only one who saw ruin ahead. Listen to this, Mr. Speaker. I refer to page 2834 of Hansard for December 19, 1962:
There is, I believe, no precedent in our parliamentary history for a government asking for the tenth monthly instalment of the total expenditures for a year before one single item of annual expenditure has been voted by parliament-not one. This is something that has not happened before in our parliamentary history . . .
It is a traditional and fundamental right of parliament to vote taxes before they are collected and to approve expenditures before they are made. When these rights are ignored, when they are violated, parliament itself is being violated and we are taking a step towards its destruction. No matter how wide a circulation we give and no matter in what form, to the Bill of Rights, and no matter how much we may talk about Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights, no matter how emotionally we may wrap ourselves up in parliamentary or national flags, both these rights I have mentioned are being deliberately and systematically violated by the present government.
I hope those words are again placed on Hansard by the person who used them on December 19, 1962, because, when we were asking at that time for interim supply for the tenth month of the fiscal year, according to him stark ruin lay ahead of us and the rights

Mr. Speaker, I do want to point out for this group that the proposals ask for a tremendous surrender by the members of this house of their rights and responsibilities. We still have five supply motions which have a place in our parliamentary system. Except for two or three departments which have been opened, we still have to bring in all the departments. The purpose of going through estimates is not only to pass sums of money but to provide members with an opportunity to question ministers regarding policies and programs, and to ascertain something about the working of each department. What we are being asked to do is to surrender all of this and to pass in a lump sum great quantities of money without any opportunity for a thorough investigation of the work of the departments.
Perhaps the hon. member who spoke those words on January 21, 1963, would like to put them on the record during the course of this debate. I refer to the hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). That is the view he held of the desperate situation that the house faced in being asked for supply for the tenth month of the fiscal year and subsequently being asked in January for the telescoping of the remaining supply motions so that we could get on with the business of the country.
What is the attitude of these hon. gentlemen in February, 1966, three years later? Are the dangers still as apparent to them now as they were then or have things changed? Is the present government to be trusted to the extent of getting a blank cheque for 11 months of the fiscal year, and perhaps for the twelfth month, without reducing the power of parliament to a nonentity? That is the situation, Mr. Speaker.
I would have thought that the Liberal party, having had the experience of the session of 1962-63 and facing a similar situation now in the period 1965-66, would have taken some precautions but its members took no precautions whatsoever. During the last three years that we were in office members of the Liberal party paid scant regard to the function of parliament and during the session of 1962-63 they did their level best to drag parliament down by calculated obstruction.

However, now they are caught in their own trap. Three years have gone by. We could treat them exactly as they treated us but we are much more responsible. We have a higher regard for parliament.
Despite the experience of the past, what was the conduct of business when the house opened last session in April and concluded at the end of June? We spent 53 days in that session and, of course, anticipated resuming on September 27. But how were those 53 days spent? It is rather interesting to look at the record. Seven days were spent on the opening and the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, which is quite normal. Six days were spent on the Budget, which is also quite normal. The Budget resolutions and the bills founded on them took seven days. Nobody can object to that. These are important financial matters affecting the Income Tax Act, the Customs Act, the Customs Tariff Act and so on.
We spent five days on the Bank Act and on the National Housing Act. There can be no objection to that at all. On various other matters affecting the setting up of an Indian Claims Commission and on four or .five items dealing with veterans legislation the house spent four days. There is no objection to that either. That is a sensible use of time.
We had one supply motion which took two days. Nine departments were called, which was a concession on our part. Normally only six are called but we said, "Call nine; let us get on with the business". Following that we spent one day on main estimates. We took the Department of External Affairs, had one day on the first item of that department and then referred the departmental estimates to a committee non-existent at the time but which was set up later.
In June we spent part of a day on interim supply and granted the government four months interim supply. Where did the rest of the time go? Instead of being spent on the main estimates during that period from April to June, how did the government organize its business? Very badly. We spent five days on the subject of the retirement of senators. Important as the other chamber is, I doubt very much that the national interest would have suffered one bit had that bill been postponed or shelved for a year or two and then brought forward. But instead of dealing with the estimates, the expenditure of money, this is what we spent our time on at the instance of the government. It was not at our request whatsoever.
February 1, 1966

Fifteen days were spent by the house on a discussion of rules and procedure. That again was at the instance of the government which wanted to shackle parliament so that it would have control in the future. We agreed on 90 per cent of the changes that were proposed but the government stubbornly insisted on forcing through certain controversial items including a report from the committee and a resolution brought forward by the government.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
On June 3, the thirty fifth day of that particular session, I had this to say as found on page 1938 of Hansard:
-I have suggested, and I repeat it, that we should remove the noncontroversial parts of this resolution-
It referred to rules and procedures. I then continued:
-get the committees set up, get the estimates referred to them and let us get on, as everybody talks about, with the business of the house. This is June 3 and it is the thirty fifth day of this session. Not a single committee has been set up. Not an estimate has been referred to an existing committee. We had an abortive motion the other day referring estimates to a committee that is not in existence.
That is how those days from April to June 3 were spent in this house. The estimates were disregarded as being unimportant and the government asked for a blank cheque through interim supply. Let us see what happened after the election on November 8 last year. Why did the Prime Minister not do what he had done in 1963? In 1963 the election was over on April 8 and we were out and the Liberals were in. The house opened on May 16, 37 days after the election, and the Prime Minister came storming in here with a hastily assembled cabinet and promised us 60 days of decision and plans to excite the daring. Then, of course, thanks to the former minister of finance-

Perhaps facing his own supporters was more fearful to him than facing the house.
I say there was failure on the part of the government to deal with the business of the house properly during the session from April to June of 1965. I say there was also failure on the part of the government in not having reassembled the house shortly after the election, for it could have been assembled on December 14 or 15. We could have dealt with the Speech from the Throne before Christmas. We could have come back shortly after Christmas or immediately after the new year. There is precedent for this. Prime Minister St. Laurent graciously consented to adjourn this house on December 21 of 1952 and we were back here in this chamber on December 27. That is the length of time we had off in 1952 and we could have done the same thing this year without that long gap between last July and January of this year. The Prime Minister waited for six and a half months before reassembling parliament.
The Prime Minister has now got himself boxed in. All the estimates of 1965-66 have to be approved and interim supply has to be sought in respect of the eleventh month. It was a tremendously dangerous thing in December of 1962 when we asked for interim supply for the tenth month. That was shocking then but now the government is asking for the same thing for the eleventh month. We are now in this position, Mr. Speaker. That was irresponsible, but that course of action is open to this house right now. A failure to grant interim supply for the month of February would, according to the Minister of Transport, compel the government to relinquish its position and refer the matter to the people. That was the policy advocated by the Liberal party at that time. I am reliably informed that the closest adviser to the Prime Minister at that time told members of the press gallery that it was the purpose of the Liberal party to force us to go to the country when we had to ask for interim supply for the eleventh month. That is the prospect that will face the government next month. Of course, we will hear from some of their supporters who will say that this is not right because we are here to carry out the business of the country.
I heard those words from the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) on February 4, 1963. He said before the supper hour: We are going to co-operate with the government. After the supper hour he had changed his mind, not for the reason that was given by the member at that time for York South. It was not a change of mind because of something he had eaten but because of directions he had received from a higher authority. If the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) would disclose here in the House of Commons so it could be recorded on Hansard what he told us behind the curtains and in the lobby we would then have an accurate account of what happened to the hon. member for Red Deer during the supper interval from six to eight o'clock on February 4, 1963.
This is the tenuous thread on which the government is existing at the present time. When interim supply is asked for next week for the eleventh month, what is the hon. member for Red Deer going to say? He will say that we are here to get on with the

business of the country, that the people have sent us here for that purpose. During the election the people never realized that the balance of power was going to rest in the hands of the hon. member for Red Deer or they certainly would not have acted as they did. A return to the country to get different advice might be very acceptable.

subtopic: ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION IN TRUCKING STRIKE
speechtext: The hon. member for York South.

subtopic: ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION IN TRUCKING STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that we, in this house, are here to study and try to solve numerous domestic problems as well as problems related to federalism and poverty. There are more than pockets of poverty here and there and everyone knows that millions of Canadians are forced to live in misery in all provinces, in all ridings, in short, in all cities of Canada.
I know also that we must face other domestic problems. Nevertheless, in view of recent events, it is important, in my opinion, to speak today about the dangerous war which is going on in Viet Nam.

Mr. Speaker, my first words on that subject, and I pick them carefully, are to say that we of the New Democratic party regret and condemn the resumption of the bombing of North Viet Nam by the United States. We condemn that action as unfortunate and reckless since it is likely to postpone for many years the possibility of a negotiated settlement.
I have noticed since being in this house and also from reading reports outside the house that every time one seeks to criticize American policy in Viet Nam one is accused by spokesmen for the government of being irresponsible. Indeed, it reminds me of a statement made some months ago in the
Supply-Mr. Lewis
opening words of an article by Professor Hans J. Morgenthau:
It illuminates the many misunderstandings that beset our Viet Nam policy that in order to criticize that policy in public one has first to justify one's right to do so.
I do not propose to justify my right and the right of my colleagues in the New Democratic party to criticize American policy. We consider it a fundamental right of anyone in Canada and particularly those of us who have the opportunity to serve in this chamber.

subtopic: ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION IN TRUCKING STRIKE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION IN TRUCKING STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we reject categorically the proposition that friendship toward a powerful neighbour means subservience. We assert that genuine friendship toward any nation shows a much deeper and greater respect when the person showing that friendship has the courage and the wisdom to point out his neighbour's errors.
We know, as every member in this house knows, that Canada's membership in the western alliance is natural and right and that American leadership of that alliance is natural and inevitable. But these facts lead to the conclusion that American actions anywhere are of immediate and direct concern to us in Canada as they are to the people of every other nation of the alliance. To take refuge, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) did yesterday, in the proposition that we are not directly involved in the war in Viet Nam and that we must therefore leave it to them who are is an escape from reality and a disservice to the integrity and purpose of the western alliance.
It has always seemed to me, Mr. Speaker, that there is a very urgent reason why Canada in particular should speak out forthrightly and with determination on these international subjects. We have had a great reservoir of good will among the new nations of the world in Africa and Asia. That good will stems from the fact that we are a nation without the stigma of colonial rule or economic domination over other peoples. This has enabled us to play an invaluable role in international affairs.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, to hon. members and particularly to the ministers of the crown that this reservoir of good will will be depleted if our role in international affairs is merely that of a satellite of one of the big powers. I share the pride which all Canadians share in the part which our Prime Minister played recently in the conference in



February 1, 1966
Supply-Mr. Lewis
Lagos on Rhodesia, a conference which began in division and ended in understanding. It would be a great pity, I suggest, if that good will were dissipated by perpetuating the kind of unnecessary timidity that our government displays in other directions.
Government spokesmen have informed the house that they have let American leaders know Canada's position on the escalation of the war in Viet Nam. All I can say is that if the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and other representatives of Canada expressed themselves in Washington in the same tepid, timid, uninspired and uninspiring tones which they have used in explaining their position on the floor of this house, no wonder Washington paid no attention to what they had to say.
When we are discussing the war in Viet Nam I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we have to consider and answer the following four questions. First, how did the United States intervention in Viet Nam first occur? Second, what are the purposes and objectives of that intervention? Third, are those purposes, if we can find out what they are, desirable in the total picture? Fourth, are they attainable through military action in Viet Nam?
It is important, sir, to recall the early events because myths have been built up about American participation in Viet Nam. Thus, President Johnson in his State of the Union message in January, 1965, said:
We are there-
That is to say, in Viet Nam:
-first because a friendly nation has asked us for help against Communist aggression. Ten years ago we pledged our help. Three Presidents have supported that pledge. We will not break it.
That is what President Johnson said. On April 7, 1965, he elaborated on that by saying:
Why are we in South Viet Nam? We are there because we have a promise to keep. Since 1954 every American President has offered support to the people of South Viet Nam.
And so on. I say with the greatest respect that this myth enunciated by President Johnson takes liberties with historical fact. The United States entered the picture in Viet Nam away back in 1947 by trying to assist in the war that the French were losing.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
In any case, the first offer of help to South Viet Nam was made by President Eisenhower to the late President Diem and was contained in a letter from the former to the latter dated

October 23, 1954. As set out in the Congressional Record of January 14, 1966, President Eisenhower said the following among other things:
Your recent requests for aid to assist in the formidable project of the movement of several hundred thousand loyal Vietnamese citizens away from areas which are passing under a de facto rule and political ideology which they abhor are being fulfilled. I am glad that the United States is able to assist in this humanitarian effort.
Later in that letter President Eisenhower said:
We have been exploring ways and means to permit our aid to Viet Nam to be more effective and to make a greater contribution to the welfare and stability of the government of Viet Nam.
Still further on the President said:
The purpose of this offer is to assist the government of Viet Nam in developing and maintaining a strong, viable state capable of resisting attempted subversion or aggression through military means.
No suggestion anywhere in that letter, Mr. Speaker, of military participation by the United States. At that time there were only some 300 or 400 United States military advisers in Viet Nam. Indeed, on February 10, 1954, President Eisenhower is reported to have stated that he-
-could conceive no greater tragedy than for the United States to become involved in all-out war in Indochina.
This is the state into which President Johnson said he was invited by a government. Let us see what another President of the United States, the late President Kennedy, said on September 2, 1963. These were his words:
In the final analysis, it is their war. They are the ones who have to win it or lose it. We can give them equipment, we can send our men out there as advisers, but they have to win it-the people of Viet Nam-against the communists. We are prepared to continue to assist them, but I don't think that the war can be won unless the people support the effort, and, in my opinion, in the last two months the government has gotten out of touch with the people.
The late President could have added that in the last few years the government of the late Diem had gotten out of touch with the people of Viet Nam. However, President Kennedy had increased the number of military advisers in Viet Nam from some few hundred to about 15,000. There is no doubt in my mind, nor in the mind of any other objective observer, that this build-up of so-called military advisers from the United States to 15,000 or more must have stimulated the build-up of North Vietnamese military help. No doubt about it, this was escalation of the war by the United States.
February X, 1966

Let us leave all the fancy words and invalid myths alone and face what happened in Viet Nam. Despite the expenditure of billions of dollars by the United States the Viet Cong continued to register victory. The government of South Viet Nam became poor and weak. President Diem was assassinated and there followed a period of instability. It was in that context, in that situation of the disintegration of the government of South Viet Nam and the failure of that government to achieve military victory, that the United States entered the war in force. And in February, 1965, the bombing of North Viet Nam began.
I say it is utterly absurd and a misreading of the relevant facts to pretend that the United States military intervention in Viet Nam was the result of an invitation from a friendly government. I have no doubt but that the unstable, fearful government of South Viet Nam was glad to welcome United States military intervention, but the effective demand for it was made by certain quarters in Washington and by the United States military leaders in Saigon rather than the people of Viet Nam. It was, Mr. Speaker, a selfinduced invitation, so tragically characteristic of every Big Power intervention in history.
The United States intervened, and what has it said are its objectives? Its objectives, Mr. Speaker, are stated in various ways and appear to be completely irreconcilable when stated by different members of the President's cabinet. The Secretary of State for the United States has generally taken the position that the United States military mission in Viet Nam is there solely for the purpose of protecting the independence of the people of Viet Nam. The Secretary of Defence of the United States has stated a different objective. He has said:
-the choice is not simply whether to continue our efforts to keep South Viet Nam free and independent, but rather, whether to continue our struggle to halt communist expansion in Asia.
My colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), pointed out these irreconcilable statements to the house the other day. Of course, if you are in Viet Nam merely for the purpose of protecting the independence of the people of Viet Nam, then you have said that you have undertaken a limited war which will be ended immediately some kind of peace settlement is reached in Viet Nam. If you take the second view, that your reason for being in South Viet Nam is to fight communism in Asia, then in effect you have undertaken to retain your forces in
Supply-Mr. Lewis
South Viet Nam indefinitely. The two objectives, therefore, are entirely irreconcilable. Indeed, as Professor Morgenthau has pointed out, this thoughtless, this reckless attempt to contain Chinese communism by peripheral engagement is bound to fail. It may be that in some minds the real intention is to provoke a war with China itself, with all the terrible consequences that would follow therefrom.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, the pretention that the United States is now in South Viet Nam in order to protect the independence of the country is in direct contradiction to the Geneva agreement of 1954. I point this out to the Secretary of State for External Affairs in view of something he said at another time. The Geneva agreement of 1954, and I ask hon. members to bear this in mind when listening to the unhappy propaganda from south of the line as echoed in this house by representatives of the government, states in section 6:
The conference recognizes that the essential purpose of the agreement relating to Viet Nam is to settle military questions with a view to ending hostilities and that the military demarcation line is provisional and should not in any way be interpreted as constituting a political or territorial boundary.
In section 7 without taking the time to read it, there is provision for a free general election to take place by July, 1956, for the purpose of uniting that country if the people of that country should so wish. When 1956 came the government of South Viet Nam, the United States and the government of North Viet Nam all feared the results of free elections and they were not held.
May I point out also that although the government of the United States was not a signatory to the agreement to which I have just referred, it made a unilateral declaration. Mr. Walter Bedell Smith made a unilateral declaration on behalf of the United States on July 21, 1954, and amongst other things the United States government stood by the declarations of the agreement in paragraph 1, namely, to refrain from the threat of the use of force.
Listen to these words in the light of what has happened and what is happening today in that unhappy part of the world: The United States would-
-view any renewal of the aggression in violation of the aforesaid agreements with grave concern and as seriously threatening international peace and security.

February 1, 1966
Supply-Mr. Lewis
In connection with the statement in the declaration concerning free elections the United States said:
In the case of nations now divided against their will, we shall continue to seek to achieve unity through free elections, supervised by the United Nations to ensure that they are conducted fairly.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
This was the agreement. This was the declaration by the United States in 1954. To take the position now that there is a de facto division which must remain forever in Viet Nam is clearly a contradiction of that undertaking. This cynicism I say, with great respect, Mr. Speaker, is compounded today when it is declared by the President of the United States that that country is prepared to negotiate for peace on the basis of the Geneva agreement in one breath and in the next breath declares that South Viet Nam must remain independent and separate. You cannot have both. You either have the Geneva agreement, in which case there are free elections in both North and South Viet Nam, or you are going to have a completely new agreement, which may well be and in the present situation probably is the only result that can be achieved today, at least for the time being.
The most tragic fact and the main reason why so many of us are unhappy about United States policy, and by that I mean United States policy in Viet Nam, is that all the best information indicates that it is almost certain to fail. Thus we have the famous Mansfield report, a report made after Senator Mansfield, the majority leader in the United States Senate and a number of other senators had spent some weeks investigating the situation on the spot. American intervention and bombing had gone on for more than one year and some 10 months when this report was made, but in it Senator Mansfield states:
-the over-all control of the country remains about the same as it was at the beginning of 1965.
Before United States military intervention, and before the bombing of North Viet Nam-

subtopic: ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION IN TRUCKING STRIKE
speechtext: Is it a majority report?

subtopic: ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION IN TRUCKING STRIKE
speechtext:
There is only one report. There is no majority or minority; there is only one report from all members of the delegation.
Then the report goes further and says:
In general, however, what the Saigon government held in the way of terrain in the early months of 1965-

I ask hon. members to note the following parenthesis:
- (and it was already considerably less than was held at the time of the assassination of Ngo Dinh Diem), is still held. What was controlled then by the Viet Cong is still controlled by the Viet Cong. What lay between was contested at the outset of 1965 and is still contested.
In simple English, despite the escalation of the war, despite the bombing of Viet Nam, there has been no progress at all in Viet Nam. The situation was then as bad for the United States side as it had been at the beginning of 1965. And why is that, Mr. Speaker? The report indicates the reason. At another spot the report says:
In so far as the military situation is concerned, the large scale introduction of United States forces and their entry into combat has blunted but not turned back the drive of the Viet Cong. The latter have responded to the increased American role with a further strengthening of their forces by local recruitment in the south and reinforcements from the north and a general stepping up of military activity. As a result the lines remain drawn in South Viet Nam in substantially the same pattern as they were at the outset of the increased U.S. commitment. What has changed basically is the scope and intensity of the struggle and the part which is being played by the forces of the United States and those of North Viet Nam.
And at another spot in the report there is this most important, and significant statement:
In short, such choices as may be open are not simple choices. They are difficult and painful choices and they are beset with many imponderables. The situation, as it now appears, offers only the very slim prospect of a just settlement by negotiations or the alternative prospect of a continuance of the conflict in the direction of a general war on the Asian mainland.
That is where, in the opinion of Senator Mansfield and his associates, the present United States policy in Viet Nam may lead us.
It is clear to me, Mr. Speaker, that the military do not believe either that they can win the war in Viet Nam by using the present forces. It may well be that they deliberately intend a massive escalation that may endanger the whole of Asia.
I want to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that not one of us in the New Democratic party has any illusions about the objectives of Communist China or about the objective of Ho Chi Minh in North Viet Nam. Nobody in this house has to tell members of this party of the importance of countering Communist aggressiveness anywhere in the world.
The argument is not whether Communist aims should be appropriately countered but how this can be done most successfully and
February 1, 1966

most effectively. I do not pretend to be an expert any more than anyone else does. However, I respectfully suggest that the escalation of the war in North Viet Nam is a dangerous and probably the most ineffective way of countering Communist expansion in Asia. Indeed, it has even seemed to me, as it has been pointed out by many commentators, that it may be self-defeating as far as that purpose is concerned.
It seems to be clear to me that Chinese leaders must be delighted with the United States escalation. The indignation which Chinese leaders show is in my view entirely contrived. I am confident that the leaders of China greet with joy the opportunity of painting the American "imperialists" in the lurid colours that they delight in painting such accusations in their propaganda.
The Mansfield report in another place points out the apprehension felt in many Asiatic countries and among many Asian peoples as the result of the escalation of the war in Viet Nam. In my view, and I say this with respect and conviction, it is not an exaggeration to say that the United States escalation of the war in Viet Nam is actually assisting the spread of Communism in Asia, and in Africa, rather than containing it.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this United States policy is placing the Soviet Union in an impossible position precisely at a time when the Soviet bloc and the western bloc are drawing closer together, when there is a real opportunity to bring about a thaw in the cold war. It must be obvious to anyone, it seems to me, that the pressures on the Soviet Union to assist North Viet Nam in view of the United States bombing attacks must be tremendous. It is equally obvious that the Soviet Union cannot for long maintain its halfhearted assistance to North Viet Nam without forfeiting to the Chinese Communists leadership in many parts of the world. Is this a wise foreign policy when it results in jeopardizing the first opportunity for some kind of real entente with the Soviet Union? Is this the way to counter an expanding and aggressive Chinese Communism?
These reasons, I submit, are cogent reasons for criticizing the policy of the United States at the present time. I add that it is particularly important to do so at the present time inasmuch as in the United States itself there is growing opposition to the policies of the administration. The revolt of a large group of senators and other political leaders in the United States is of great significance.
Supply-Mr. Lewis
The foreign relations committee chaired by Senator Fulbright questioned the Secretary of State of that country the other day. During the questioning Senator Fulbright said that it had to be determined whether the current United States position in Viet Nam was the result of stepping into a colonial war on the wrong side.
Senator Clarke, at the same session, said: "Personally, I am scared to death that we are on the way to world war three". And Senator Gore added that "many people do not believe, and many members of congress do not believe, that the dangers of nuclear war with China and Russia implicit in the Viet Nam fighting are worth the effort". These Senators spoke for an increasing number of Americans.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
There is a growing understanding among more and more people that the basis for the war in Viet Nam was founded upon a civil war. In a speech to the United States Senate on January 14 last Senator Young of Ohio made the following statement, and I want to quote it verbatim because it seems to me terribly significant. He said:
From September 28 to last October 20-
That would be last year.
-I was in southeast Asia most of the time. I went, looked, and listened. Very soon I learned we are involved in a civil war over there. In South Viet Nam I was at every airbase except one-travelling through the entire area by helicopter, airplane, and jeep. It was my considered judgment that South Viet Nam is of no strategic importance whatever to the defence of the United States. Furthermore, the fact is that the conflict raging in Viet Nam is a civil war. General Westmorland stated to me that the bulk of the Viet Cong fighting in South Viet Nam were born and reared in South Viet Nam. General Stilwell, in Thailand, went further. He stated that 80 per cent of the Viet Cong fighting in the Mekong Delta area south of Saigon, were bom and reared in that area. They were not infiltrators or Communists from the north.
I do not deny that there is not ample evidence that there has been some infiltration from the north. It is the nature of communism to take advantage of every disturbance in every area of discontent, and it would have been silly to expect that North Viet Nam and China would not take advantage of the civil war in Viet Nam. But basically this was a civil war in its beginning and because of that it is impossible for the armies of the United States to win the present war against the Viet Cong. This is the reason the guerilla fighting goes on with such devotion and courage and it is why the Viet Cong, it is almost

February 1, 1966
Supply-Mr. Lewis
universally agreed, has the support of the people on the farms and in the villages of South Viet Nam.
We, Mr. Speaker, like the rest of the world, greeted with relief and hope the pause in the fighting which President Johnson called some time ago. We all hoped that the peace offensive would succeed. But all of us knew that it would not be easy to get the parties to the conference table. No one thought it could be done in the first month of the try. Indeed, Mr. Walter Lippman stated in an article a few days ago that he thought the peace offensive was bound, temporarily, to fail.
I put on record now part of a statement issued on January 16 by the federal council of the New Democratic party on the subject of Viet Nam. We said in that statement that "it would be a tragedy if lack of early success in the search for negotiations were used as an excuse to intensify or to continue the war." That tragedy, Mr. Speaker, has occurred. Bombing of North Viet Nam by the United States has been resumed despite the fact that many responsible people, including the Pope and spokemen in congress in the United States, believed that the search for peace should have continued, and also despite the fact that the President admitted on January 13 at a press conference that military activity in the Vietnamese war by the other side had been reduced some.
The plea for a further search for peace was made with typical restraint in an editorial in the New York Times of January 30, an editorial which concluded, as my friend the hon. member for Greenwood pointed out the other day, with these sentences:
Neither the possibilities for peace nor the exercise of diplomatic ingenuity have been exhausted. The resumption of the bombing of North Viet Nam now would sacrifice still greater diplomatic assets for relatively minor military gains.
This is what the resumption of bombing of North Viet Nam has meant, and this is why I respectfully say that it may well mean a postponement for years of the possibility of a peaceable settlement.
At the same time as the United States has intensified its war effort on North Viet Nam it has brought the matter before the Security Council of the United Nations this morning. Let me suggest in passing that if Russia or China had ever come to the Security Council in a search for peace at the same moment as they had intensified a war, Washington would have been the first to accuse them of insincerity and cynicism. An editorial in today's

Le Devoir states it more politely. The editorial says in part:

It may be assumed that the White House took this second initiative in order to soften the impact felt by the world because of the resumption of bombings, and also to satisfy in part the enemies of escalation. The "hawks" are placated by the resumption of bombings while the "doves" are offered what may in some respects be considered a continuation of the peace offensive.

This kind of cynicism, Mr. Speaker, is unforgiveable in a great country like the United States.
Despite one's fears and doubts, and these are my final words, about the approach to the Security Council, we in the New Democratic party nevertheless hope that the Security Council of the United Nations will utilize this opportunity to take the initiative to seek a settlement before it is too late. I understand from speaking to members of the press that this morning the Soviet and French delegates opposed any action by the Security Council. May I express regret that they did so and suggest that instead of opposing any action by the Security Council of the United Nations they would have better served the world and peace if they had required the United States to stop its bombing of North Viet Nam forthwith as a condition for the United Nations entering into any action to seek a settlement. I hope that this will still be done and that the United Nations will take any and all steps to bring all interested parties, including the National Liberation Front, North Viet Nam and China, to the conference table.
I appeal to the government to be more firm and more forthright, in speaking for this parliament and for this country, in trying to persuade our friend and ally to the south of the folly of its present policies. Such a forthright appeal would strengthen the hands of the responsible elements in the United States and again awaken the respect and the good will in the nations of the world toward Canada, particularly in Asia and Africa.
At all events, whatever may be the immediate results, it is our duty to speak out against the reckless military adventure in Viet Nam, an adventure which not only prolongs and intensifies the suffering of the unfortunate Vietnamese but also menaces the peace of the world and the cause of democracy in Asia. It is impossible, surely, for the Asians to regard the war in Viet Nam as anything other than a war between the whites and the Asians. With the United States armed forces now numbering some

200,000	and likely to go to 300,000 or 400,000, the U.S. participation is becoming that of conducting a full-scale war without a declaration of war against North Viet Nam, carrying with it the danger of a world holocaust in the present terrible age of nuclear destruction.

Supply-Hon. P. Martin of Canada and the policy of the United States with regard to this matter. All one has to do is examine the 1962 majority report of the International Commission on which Canada serves with India and Poland in order to find a demonstration of what I have said. Likewise I would recall to the hon. member that on February 17, 1965, Canada appended a minority report to the majority report then proposed by our colleagues on the commission, India and Poland. We submitted this minority report not because we took exception to the majority report but because we thought that since it was confined to air strikes in the north the majority report did not present a balanced picture of the facts. But if anyone wants evidence of our independence of judgment and of decision I ask him to note the findings of the majority report of 1962 wherein Canada joined with India in a citation of acts which we felt were in violation of the Geneva agreement, acts committed not only by the north but by the south and by the country which had been asked under article 51 of the United Nations charter to assist South Viet Nam in defending itself against aggression and against infiltration from the north.
So the record is clear that Canada has passed judgment, a judgment based on 11 years experience in Indochina on three commissions, those in Cambodia and in Laos as well as that in Viet Nam. The hon. gentleman has said that our resistance to some developments in United States foreign policy was lacking in vigour, that it was not as active as it should have been. He is an experienced lawyer. He knows a good bit about international problems. He is among the last in this house who should suggest that the most effective way of expressing disagreement with a neighbour, particularly one associated in an alliance, is necessarily by making wide, unlimited accusations in public. There are more effective ways of expressing one's opinion than by publicly criticizing a country with which Canada is so much in agreement and for which Canada has such great admiration, a country, moreover, with which Canada has such close economic ties and other interests. I suggest we would do disservice to the promulgation of a sound foreign policy by resorting to irresponsible public criticism instead of to the methods by which the government is now making its views known to the government of the United States, views which have been made known even within very recent hours and days.

It seems to me that we could stop talking about conflicts, not only in Viet Nam, but in all parts of the world. Nowadays, we do not know; we are building a new Tower of Babel; nobody understands anything any longer. A new Tower of Babel yes, exactly, because pride has replaced good faith. Nations are guided by pride, and the people pay for the pride of certain irresponsible leaders who hold absolute power in a great many countries at this time.
Mr. Speaker, as I said a while ago, I do not intend to deal at length with the Viet Nam question.
Today, at noon, I put a question to the future Minister of Manpower (Mr. Marchand) concerning winter works. The Minister was telling us that the total sum requested by the province of Quebec for winter works was $23.7 million and that of that sum, $23.5 million have already been paid. Only $200,000 more would remain to be paid according to the winter works agreement between the federal and the provincial governments.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell hon. members, who probably have to face similar problems in their respective ridings, what is happening in mine.
I get telephone calls from municipalities that are organized and from others that are not but which, nevertheless, benefit from the winter works program. Now, the mayor of such and such a municipality tells me that, for the past six, seven or eight months-in some cases, for the past two years-he has not received the money to pay for the winter works carried out in his municipality and that he called the Quebec Department of Labour to protest or claim the money. You know that our municipalities have to borrow from the bank or the "caisse populaire" and must pay interest.
Now, the answer from Quebec is sure to be that the government in Ottawa did not send the money and is behind in its payments.
Well, each time I got in touch with the federal Department of Labour, I was told that the government in Ottawa had most certainly paid its share to the province of Quebec.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
But the province does not pay those municipalities. Why? Because it must contribute, in all cases, 40 per cent of the cost of winter works carried out by the municipalities, and since it has no money, the province puts off paying the municipalities for winter works and then puts the blame on the federal government.
That is what we wanted to point out to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) this afternoon.

subtopic: ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION IN TRUCKING STRIKE
speechtext: It is true.

subtopic: ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR INTERVENTION IN TRUCKING STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we would like to know why the federal government does not make an enquiry, when it gives that money to the province of Quebec, to find out if the province really uses that money to pay the municipalities. In other cases, when the municipality submits its projects to the provincial government, the latter, probably in order to minimize the results or to hide a little what is happening keeps the accounts for a few months because it cannot pay the 40 per cent which it undertook to pay and, consequently, delays the projects. Enquiries are then made to the federal government which answers: "We did not get any account or bill from the province". That is true.
February 1, 1966

However, that constitutes an injustice toward our municipalities, our non-incorporated parishes which benefit from such winter works. They are obliged to pay interests for months because the Quebec ministers of municipal affairs or labour do not tell the truth to the municipal authorities.
Mr. Speaker, there are different ways for the provincial government not to pay but the reason is always the one I gave a while ago, namely that the government does not have the money needed to pay the 40 per cent and, moreover, it uses the 50 or 60 per cent that the federal government pays to Quebec on behalf of the municipalities and for months and months that money is used for other things, without the federal government's knowledge.
The minister tells us that he is not aware of that situation and states: "We pay and after that it is none of our business." The same thing happens when we ask: "Do you help the municipalities when they are obliged to borrow?" The minister then answers: "The municipalities do not know it." But not much publicity is done to tell the municipalities how they can get loans that would help them, when they need them so badly. Why is not more publicity done about the benefits that the municipalities could get under the existing federal legislation?
Mr. Speaker, I set aside the matter of winter works for a few minutes to go back to the speech made yesterday by the member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) whom I now see in his place. In his constructive speech, he told us among other things that Quebec was a special province, that centralization within the national administration was absolutely necessary, that our labour force was inadequate at the present time if we wanted to increase the country's productivity, that he had become aware that incomes were inadequate in his riding-a rather important point-and that access to the labour market was becoming increasingly difficult for unskilled labour.
Mr. Speaker, with regard to his statement that Quebec is a special province, everyone in this house takes pleasure in repeating it. In fact, all we hear is that Quebec is not like the others; that it must be treated differently; that Quebec is a special province, that Quebec is this, that Quebec is that.
Of course, Quebec mentality is a Latin French Canadian mentality. The whole of Canada, outside Quebec, is Anglo-Saxon and the English language has priority there. In
Supply-Mr. Caouette
this regard, I read in the January 29 issue of the newspaper Le Droit the following statement made in Toronto by the former mayor of Ottawa and I quote:
Miss Charlotte Whitton, the former mayor of Ottawa stated that an independent Quebec would be better than a Canada ruled by the French Canadian minority.
In a speech delivered to the Association for lands and farms improvement of Ontario, Dr. Whitton gave a brief outline of Canada of today and tomorrow.
Next year will be the end of the first and last century of confederation, she stated.
She added that the British North America Act advocates justice and that Canada must abide by the conditions of its contract.
Dr. Whitton pointed out that the Quebec population only made up 12 per cent of the whole Canadian population.
The other 88 per cent cannot be expected to hand over control of public services and private businesses to that minority.
You cannot run a nation that way.
If this thing comes to a head, we would be better off with two independent states rather than have a sham state.
Mr. Speaker, it is inconceivable that in 1966 some people still have it in their heads or still think that the French Canadian Quebec minority would like to run practically the whole country or 88 per cent of the population.
Even though we must accept the fact-we accept it and proclaim it in a loud voice-that Quebec is not a province like the others, nevertheless, when Quebec demands something, people think right away that provinces with English majorities, such as Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, are going to be deprived of something.
Such is not the situation in Quebec. For instance, when some provincial ministers are heard to demand the priority of the French language in Quebec, nobody is against it. But what would be the reaction if the priority of French were required in Toronto, Winnipeg, Hamilton or London? We do not ask for such things; we are only asking for what belongs to us. In our province, we do not discriminate against other people.
When I want to speak English in my riding, I speak English. When I want to speak English in Montreal, I speak English. But the fact remains that Quebec is a French province within confederation and it is the only one.
Ontario is an English province. The other provinces of Canada are also English. Are we

February 1, 1966
Supply-Mr. Caouette
trying to impose Quebec's views on the whole population? No, Mr. Speaker. Such is not the case.
There are still narrow-minded people in the country who hamper understanding and agreement between the two ethnic groups, between French and English speaking Canada. We have never asked tor anything of the kind. It is being stated in Toronto that a 12 per cent minority would like to lord it over 88 per cent of Canada's population.
When the fight British Columbia is waging to control the Columbia river development is considered, has it ever occurred to anyone to represent the British Columbia Social Crediters as separatists? No. But as soon as we demand something for Quebec, a hue and cry is raised.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
There is a limit to everything. There must be an end to those charges. The province of Quebec asks for nothing that belongs to others. The province of Quebec asks for the power to administer itself, to mind its own business, to organize on its own the development of its natural resources; that is what the province of Quebec is asking for. It does not want to get the others out of the province; to the contrary. If others can assist in this development, they are welcome in the province. Is there an hon. member, from east or west, who can state that he has been ill-treated in the province of Quebec? Certainly not. Ideas like that are expressed throughout the land, in the other provinces, to the effect that French Canadians are narrow-minded and that they want to impose the use of their language and to oblige the whole population of Canada to learn French. When the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Bicul-turalism held public hearings throughout the country it was said: They want to push French down our throats. We do not want to force anyone to learn French, Mr. Speaker; that is clear. Whether hon. members who do not want to learn French do not learn it, we could not care less. But when we wanted to learn English we learned it. We can speak both languages, not because we were forced to, but because we wanted to learn English in order to try to get to know the other ethnic group living in Canada. That is why we learned English.
The hon. member for Matapedia-Matane was right in saying that Quebec is not a province like the others. But this does not mean that Quebec wants to force herself upon the others; no, it is not that.

We sometimes hear statements from Quebec provincial ministers that are not too easy to swallow. Mind you, I do not share all the views expressed by Quebec provincial ministers, but when a minister makes a well-founded statement and speaks knowingly of things that do exist in our province, then I stand behind him 100 per cent. It is not a question of being a separatist. I was referring a moment ago to the priority of French in the province of Quebec. Who could blame us? If I were to go and open a business in Toronto, do you think I would put up French ads on my store front? No, I would use English signs to attract the local people. We blame certain firms for using English billboards in Montreal, the second largest French city in the world. They forget that the French Canadians are there. They forget there are six million of them in the province of Quebec.
I repeat that we do not wish to impose the use of French in Toronto. But others should at least have the decency of respecting us 100 per cent at home, not only for the fun of doing so, not because circumstances warrant it, but all the time. That is all we demand.
The hon. member for Matapedia-Matane went on to speak of the ever so useful centralization. I do not share his views on that point. I believe in decentralization wherever possible so that the government may be closer to the individual, to the people. Everyone knows, in our province as well as in the others, that the federal government is farther from us than are the provincial, municipal or school authorities. That is common knowledge.
Centralization in such countries as our own means growing estrangement from the people, in every regard, whether administrative or other.
Third, they say the manpower is inadequate. I have dealt rather often with this matter. During the second world war of 1939-45, when they wanted to employ those who had been unemployed for 10 years, who were not educated, who had not attended colleges or universities, because at that time it was the great depression, not one federal minister, not one Canadian economist maintained that the manpower was inadequate to manufacture shells, armaments, destroying devices, etc. At that time, everybody was welcome in war plants. It did not take too long to train them, to give them the required
February 1, 1966

knowledge to sustain a war production, which was tremendous in relation to the small population we had at that time.
There was no question of inadequate manpower to wage war. But today we are told that we have an inadequate manpower, that on the labour market employers are getting more fussy.
Every day, on television, employers are urged to hire 45-year old men who cannot find employment. Are employers so hard to please? No, but they would sooner hire young people just out of high school or university instead of men of 45 who have a family to raise and to support. And it is cheaper to hire a 22, 23 or 24-year old than a father of 45. Members as well as ministers know it is a fact. Today a man of 45 has a hard time to find a job, not because he does not have the experience or the required skill, but because at 40 he is already too old.
Through propaganda and publicity, they are urged, on the one hand, to go back to school, learn a new trade and become a mechanic, an electrician, or improve their knowledge in some other field of the Canadian economy, while, on the other hand, television is shouting "give those men a job"; the man of 45, in the prime of life, is able to render great services to his boss: he is experienced. He is told in some cases: My friend, your education is inadequate, while the young people are told: You are well educated but you lack experience. Nothing can be done with our young people, because in Canada, in 1965, in spite of existing deficiencies, national production has nevertheless increased by 8 or 9 per cent compared to 1964.
The national production may reach $55 billion in 1966. It reached $51 billion in 1965. In addition to this annual production which is renewed each year while showing a sizeable increase, existing inventories in stores and warehouses throughout Canada are not taken into account. This fact is being ignored. There is actually an over-production instead of an under-production, as the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane said last year.
So much so that 85 per cent of our workers, or our farmers-we mean the toiling working class-are involved in financing plans for three, four and five years to purchase our production of perhaps five or ten years ago.
What is lacking then is obviously this purchasing power in the hands of Canadians to
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion purchase existing products, to achieve an economic balance under which production will meet the needs of Canadian consumers.
I said not long ago, that the major problem, the number one problem in Canada is not the production problem, for it is solved. It is the distribution problem. But there are different means of distribution. It can be done by economic planning as suggested by the Socialists. It can also be done according to planning under which the government would decide what is to be distributed to each.
Our solution is to put the buying power in the hands of Canadians, of the Canadian people. It will be the Canadian people who will make their own plans and decide what to buy, who will order new production and direct future production through demand.
There is not a single member, minister or former minister who now fears of being unable to obtain clothing, food, medical care, etc. And yet, several people-none of them members of the house-are in terrible want of the strict minimum. We, Creditistes, are not miracle workers but we precisely want to put some order in the country's finances. The problem is not in the heart of man but in our present monetary system. As long as that system is not adjusted to present-day needs, no matter what legislation comes through, the economic, social and political problem of Canada will never be solved. We have a solution, and we are fighting to have it understood, both inside and outside the House of Commons, and we shall carry on this fight as long as Canadians are not assured of economic security and personal freedom.
